# How to read a research paper

Most people read papers the way they read articles: start at the beginning, go to the
end, and hope something sticks. That approach fails on papers because papers are not
written to be read linearly. They are written to satisfy reviewers, and reviewers read
the abstract, the figures, and the conclusion, in that order.

A better first pass takes about ten minutes. Read the title and abstract, then skip to
the conclusion, then look at every figure and table and read only the caption. The goal
of this pass is not to understand the paper but to decide whether it deserves a second
pass at all. Most papers do not.

The second pass takes about an hour and goes through the paper properly, but still
skips proofs and derivations. Mark anything you cannot follow without stopping. The
density of those marks tells you whether the paper is worth a third pass. A paper that
requires a third pass is rare, and usually it is because you are missing background
rather than because the paper is unclear.

When you are missing background, stop reading the paper. Go find the background first.
Reading a paper you lack the prerequisites for is the most common way to waste an
afternoon while feeling productive.

The method section deserves special treatment. It is where papers are most likely to
hide problems, and it is the section reviewers check least carefully. Look for what is
missing rather than what is there: which baselines were not compared, which datasets
were not used, which conditions were not controlled.

Take notes as questions rather than summaries. A summary is something you will never
re-read. A question is something you can answer later, and answering it is what
actually moves the knowledge into place.
